#6645. How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms

The next time someone asks ChatGPT to find them a designer handbag, the answer could be a previously owned version, even if they weren’t originally looking to shop secondhand.

Rémi Bouchez, who was appointed as Vestiaire Collective’s new CTO in March, says the resale platform is working to make its product listing available to OpenAI’s broader agentic shopping systems, which would allow secondhand pieces to appear alongside new products in AI-generated recommendations. The proposed plan follows Vestiaire Collective quietly launching a dedicated app plugin within ChatGPT last month, allowing shoppers to search its pre-owned luxury inventory and compare products using conversational prompts within the chatbot. A shopper searching for a new Prada bag could now conceivably be shown a pre-owned version at a fraction of the price, or an archival design that is no longer available firsthand.

At a time when luxury consumers are questioning rising prices, this could significantly impact the shopping journey. And this is just one part of a wider transformation in how secondhand fashion is discovered. Resale platforms are simultaneously rebuilding their own search and recommendation algorithms, using AI to understand product images, interpret shoppers’ tastes and determine which listings get seen. As a result, the rules of discovery are changing on two fronts: within resale marketplaces themselves, and through the AI assistants that could increasingly direct shoppers towards them.

Bouchez believes that if AI agents like Muse, Instinct and Duet reach mainstream adoption, it could fundamentally change how luxury shoppers weigh up their options.

“These agents are capable of ingesting a ton of information — way more than human shoppers can. They remember user preferences over time, and they can catch things like discreet terms and conditions or shady seller behaviors and put them in front of a user who would have otherwise missed them,” says Bouchez. He explains how an AI agent could compare a Prada bag across several platforms, assessing its condition, authentication details and seller reliability before recommending the best value option, raising the stakes for resellers.

It’s an opportunity resale platforms have long been waiting for. Finding a particular product secondhand has traditionally meant scrolling through multiple marketplace apps, deciphering inconsistent descriptions and comparing endless individual listings. AI now promises to take much of the legwork out of that hunt.

Across the resale industry, rival platforms are investing in both forms of discovery. Depop has enabled shoppers to search its marketplace through Apple’s Visual Intelligence on supported iPhones. Last month, The RealReal introduced its own AI shopping assistant, Ask TRR, built on Google Gemini AI that enables shoppers to search in natural language — or by uploading images of products they’ve seen for visual search — while learning shoppers’ preferences. Speaking on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Rati Levesque said Ask TRR’s early adopters spend 20% more per transaction than non-users. The RealReal is also preparing for shopping journeys that begin outside its own platform. A spokesperson tells Vogue Business the company is restructuring data on its 1.5 million listed items to make them easier for external AI agents to find and recommend.

Together, this represents an AI-driven sea change for resale. While AI may struggle to replicate the subjective judgement involved in fashion discovery, resale presents a more straightforward opportunity. A shopper searching for a particular archival bag doesn’t need their algorithm to have good taste, just to identify the right model and compare available listings by price, condition and authenticity.

Resale discovery is increasingly moving beyond keyword search. At Vestiaire Collective, visual search can now recognise multiple objects in an image and identify similar listings, while its search systems increasingly interpret natural language requests. AI can also extract information from photographs — including aspects of fit and visible defects — that previously depended on sellers filling in descriptions.

Poshmark is also using AI to bridge the gap between what sellers photograph and what shoppers can find. Its “Smart List AI” tool automatically generates searchable titles, descriptions and product categories from uploaded photographs. Chief product officer Heather Friedland says it makes listing creation less of a “heavy lift” once the photos are up, and that listing on Poshmark is now five times faster than before. Poshmark’s AI tool also automates offers, letting Poshmark negotiate with buyers on behalf of the seller, which she says makes selling 50% faster. “We want sellers to focus most on what they do best: source great items and have Poshmark take care of the rest,” she says.

At Depop, shoppers are increasingly browsing the personalized Suggested For You feed rather than starting with a search, says chief product officer Sonia Biddle. Its algorithm responds to individual preferences and emerging cultural trends, while AI identifies listings by category, color and style, making products discoverable even when sellers haven’t used precisely the right keywords.

“Fashion often starts with an idea: an era, an occasion or someone whose style you love, and that’s not always something you can put into words,” Biddle says. “AI helps us understand what you’re after, not just the words you type.” For sellers, that means some longstanding tactics like keyword hashtags may become less important, while product photography, pricing and reliability are becoming harder to ignore.

Depop’s visual search also allows shoppers to upload a photograph or screenshot — including of something spotted in a first-hand retailer — to find similar secondhand pieces. A new-season jacket might inspire a purchase, but not necessarily from the brand selling it.

Resale execs recommend sellers photograph items in natural light, capturing multiple angles and clearly showing any signs of wear. Photo: Courtesy of Depop

As images become more central to discovery, platforms are also investing in how listings look. Last month, Vestiaire announced a partnership with AI photography company Photoroom to standardise the main photograph of every new listing — around 40,000 items a day — bringing the often inconsistent images uploaded by individual sellers closer to the polished aesthetic of first-hand luxury retail.

The technology removes backgrounds, adjusts lighting, centres products and adds realistic shadows. According to results from a randomized A/B test conducted by Vestiaire Collective and Photoroom, listings processed using the new technology had a 5% higher sell-through rate than those using Vestiaire’s previous in-house photo-editing tool, while unique product page views increased by between 3% and 7%.

Next, Vestiaire is experimenting with much more ambitious AI image enhancements that can make the items themselves look more PDP shoot ready, Bouchez says, like digital ironing.

It’s a delicate balance: AI can make a pre-owned handbag look like something fit for a luxury DTC site, but an algorithm that makes a scuff disappear could also undermine the trust on which resale depends. Yet Bouchez says Vestiaire has seen an approximately 6% improvement in the proportion of enhanced listings selling within seven days since these AI image updates, without a corresponding increase in returns.

For sellers, getting discovered still depends heavily on the algorithms operating within resale marketplaces themselves. So what determines which listings appear first, and can sellers influence their ranking?

At Vestiaire, the answer isn’t simply the lowest price or the newest upload. Bouchez describes a three-stage ranking system that identifies relevant products, reorders them according to marketplace factors and then adjusts results to individual preferences. Those factors include condition, pricing, location and seller reliability. Because Vestiaire operates globally, proximity can matter: a nearby item may mean faster shipping, fewer customs complications and easier returns, which may mean it gets surfaced first.

Vestiaire assesses what constitutes a fair price according to factors including condition, location and whether the seller is a professional offering returns. An implausibly cheap luxury item may raise questions about authenticity, rather than look like an irresistible bargain. Bouchez says that analysing these factors is still a combination of humans and AI.

“Trust is a big pillar for Vestiaire — we invest a lot in that trust, on manual verification, on assessing a listing before it’s published,” he says. “Obviously, we want to keep the same level of trust but lower the investment with AI, but the more we can keep this USP high and even increase the trust, the better our position as a platform.”

Depop’s search algorithm prioritises how closely a listing matches a shopper’s query, including brand, category, size and color. Popularity signals — views, likes and additions to shopping bags — also matter, alongside seller history, location and personal shopping preferences. If a listing is underperforming, she recommends new photographs, a more detailed description and a pricing review.

Shoppers, meanwhile, are becoming more deliberate about influencing what appears in their feeds.

“It’s been really interesting hearing our community talk about ‘training their algorithm,’” Biddle says. “People know that what they like, view and save shapes what they see, and they’re becoming really deliberate about it.” But there’s a downside to this hyper-personalization: the more accurately a feed reflects established tastes, the less likely shoppers may be to encounter something unexpected.

Good product photography is increasingly important for visibility on resale platforms. Photo: Courtesy of The RealReal.

To counter AI’s tendency to reinforce existing preferences, Poshmark introduced a new “Tastemaker” programme in September, enlisting fashion figures including Courtney Grow, Colleen Allen and Jalil Johnson to curate shoppable edits from across its resale inventory. The platform has also established a dedicated human merchandising team to work alongside its AI and machine learning specialists, identifying emerging trends and bringing a more editorial approach to product recommendations.

“On trends, a purely algorithmic system tends to amplify what’s already popular,” Friedland says. “Human curation is our counterweight. Our tastemakers bring in new styles and AI then figures out which shoppers those styles will resonate with.”

For shoppers looking to escape their own personalized recommendations, Biddle suggests sorting search results by price or newest first, too. Visual search can also help uncover pieces that shoppers cannot easily describe. On Poshmark, Friedland recommends saving searches for specific archival pieces and liking items to help refine future recommendations.

And as AI agents take on more of the shopping process, the question of what consumers don’t see becomes even more significant. Vestiaire’s ChatGPT integration allows shoppers to compare up to three selected listings, asking the AI agent to explain differences in price, condition and seller information. But it also introduces another gatekeeper: instead of scrolling through hundreds of listings themselves, shoppers may increasingly rely on an AI assistant to decide which options are worth considering — and which never make it onto their shortlist.

For first-hand luxury brands, the implications go beyond losing the occasional sale to a cheaper pre-owned alternative. Resale platforms are accumulating information about which designs consumers continue to desire, years after they disappear from stores. Depop’s Biddle argues that these signals can be valuable for brands developing future collections.

“Resale tells brands something their own sales data can’t: what people still love years after it left the shop floor,” she says. “When we see searches spike for a particular era or label, it’s often an early sign that something’s coming back.”

Poshmark is similarly using AI to identify patterns across searches, listings, likes and transactions, tracking demand for particular designers, eras, silhouettes and price points. Friedland says combining these signals with scarcity and actual resale prices can help distinguish fleeting trends from enduring desirability — offering brands a measure of a product’s success beyond its initial sellthrough.

For luxury brands, the stakes are particularly high. If AI assistants can connect consumers with archival products as readily as current collections, brands may find themselves competing with their own past successes, without controlling how those products are presented or compared.

As sellers learn to level up their listings, shoppers train their feeds and luxury brands compete for attention, the question is how much influence any of them will retain over what an AI agent ultimately recommends.

#6643. How to Avoid Sports Injuries in Your 30s, 40s, and Beyond

At 38 years old, I’ve been fortunate enough to go most of my life without being bothered by sports injuries, despite being consistently and competitively active for the better part of three decades. On the soccer field, I’ve played on and off at club level since primary school. (I’m currently holding it down as a winger on my local club’s 30+ “seniors” team.)

Meanwhile, as a health journalist and all-around enthusiastic exerciser, I’ve thrown myself at countless physical challenges—mostly for fun, sometimes to help pay the rent. Marathons, trail races, triathlons, 24-hour relays, mud runs, obstacle course races, Hyrox—you name it, I was probably obsessed with it for a time. And through it all, the only injury I ever incurred was a torn meniscus (the undignified result of attempting a wildly above-my-paygrade basketball dunk on a charitably lowered rim, at a promotional event). If only the surgeon could have extracted the memory of that day along with the frayed connective tissue he removed from my knee. I’m pretty sure I was wearing jeans, too.

All of this to say, everything was smooth sailing for a very long time, until it suddenly wasn’t. Somewhere around the age of 35, for reasons beyond my comprehension at the time, the wheels started to come off the bus. First, a stress fracture to my foot. I noticed it one night in bed and couldn’t tell you when it happened. Regardless, it put me in a boot for three months.

Next, a torn hamstring during a routine game of pick-up football, making the same run I’d made so many times before. I thought I’d just pulled it, so I kept playing, which of course only made it worse. That decision cost me six months. Then a strained calf muscle at a gentle session of run club. And, finally, shin splints. I don’t even remember how many months that one took me out for, but it felt like forever.

This barrage of sports injuries—all sustained within a roughly two-year period—was unrelenting, each overlapping pang seemingly passing the baton to the next. Needless to say, I was miserable. And the worst part was that I couldn’t understand why this was happening to me. I had been maintaining the same activity level, same diet, same supplements, and the same sleeping habits.

You always hear people talking half-jokingly about how getting older takes its toll on the body. But nothing really prepares you for that moment when you start to actually experience it for yourself. It’s existential. Brutal. Depressing, honestly. Sometimes the best way to deal with these spiral-inducing moments is to simply talk to other people dealing with the same thing. So I recently asked my, er, seasoned soccer team’s group chat: What do you do to avoid and manage sports injuries as you get older?

Kevin, 40, chimes in first: “There’s no avoiding, mate. Just managing.”

“Funnily enough, I’ve actually started doing yoga, which has been great for mobility and stretching out my lower back,” writes Chris, 35, who battles with a recurring quadratus lumborum (QL) issue. “I was always a bit hesitant to give it a go—not because I didn't think it would help, but because I couldn't get past the fact that I'd essentially be following a similar exercise plan to my mum! I think that’s been one of the bigger adjustments as I’ve gotten older: accepting that looking after your body sometimes means doing things you might have previously associated with an entirely different generation.”

“For me, I think the most important thing is to keep going in general,” adds Brian, who recently turned 42. “I remember when I was around 20 years old, my manager at the time, who was in his late 30s and retired from playing, was doing some running on his own before the team training session started. The lads were joking and teasing him about making a comeback, but I remember him saying, ‘If you stop moving at my age, you won't be able to start again.’ I think that’s good advice.”

In some way, I suppose it’s comforting to know that this is something we all have to deal with, whether you’re a Sunday league bench warmer or in contention for the Ballon d’Or. "With age, there’s just a higher incidence of soft-tissue injuries as your muscles lose strength and elasticity,” says Dr. Brian Forsythe, a sports medicine surgeon, associate professor at Rush University Medical Center, and recreational soccer player himself. According to Forsythe, who also serves as head orthopedic officer for MLS team Chicago Fire FC and president of the Professional Soccer Physicians Society, over time athletes across the skill spectrum will ultimately begin running into the same injuries.

You may not be able to halt the inevitable march of time, but there are certainly ways to minimize and slow its toll on your body. This requires some work but could ultimately be the difference between hanging up your boots and kicking on for another 10, 20, or even 30 years.

“It's up to you to take some responsibility,” Forsythe says. “Think about the lifestyle you had when you were 17 or 18—how you took care of your body and what you looked like. Then look in the mirror and ask yourself, ‘How much of my life now resembles what it was then?’ If you’re going out and having a few pints, understand that that inhibits your recovery and decreases protein synthesis. If you’re overweight, that has effects beyond just not looking great in your clothes. It’s increased joint load, increased rotational torque. You’re more likely to get injured. So you have to set realistic expectations of what your body is capable of doing. But you can definitely still do a lot.”

If you’re not ready to call time just yet, here are a couple of strategies you can start implementing today, courtesy of Forsythe and a handful of other experts.

“Number one, and it should be obvious, is just general conditioning,” says Forsythe. Being a slightly less sedentary human being during the work week means you won’t send your body into total shock when you decide to get going over the weekend.

“A lot of injuries come from that mismatch between what we do all week and the intensity we demand from our bodies on the weekend,” says sports medicine physician Dr. Alex McDonald. As Dr. James B. Chen, orthopedic surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center, puts it: “The biggest risk isn't necessarily your age, but your schedule.”

“When you think about playing in your teens and twenties, you were probably close to your ideal body weight,” says Forsythe. Ideal body weight, or IBW, refers to the weight at which your body is able to function most efficiently and without a heightened risk of injury. “All of the forces across your joints are multiplied almost exponentially with additional pounds on your frame,” says Forsythe. For example, “the force across your knee can be up to six times your body weight.”

“If you've ever been overweight and you climb up and down stairs and notice that the front of your knee hurts, that's because of those increased pressures and forces,” adds Forsythe.

Jogging a couple of miles a week may help you get through your Sunday workout our pick-up game, but it’s not doing anything to prevent in-the-moment injuries. To do that, you have to train the way you play—whatever game that is. “It's changes of direction," says Forsythe. It's rapid acceleration and deceleration. It's pivoting, twisting, turning.” Basically, bring back whatever drills you used to do on your sports team when you were younger, and adjust them for the demands of the sport you currently play.

No matter how frequently and comprehensively you train, a complete warm-up before any big athletic event is a non-negotiable. "It helps dramatically, which is why you'll always see professionals warm up for 30-45 minutes before a match,” says Forsythe. When it comes to soccer, FIFA actually has developed a warm-up program, called FIFA ll+, specifically for injury prevention. “It’s a free routine that only takes about 20 minutes, and includes running drills plus strength, balance, and landing exercises such as Nordic hamstring curls and single-leg balance work,” says McDonald. “It’s been shown to cut injuries by about a third, but it needs to be done at least twice a week—ideally three or four times a week—to really reduce the risk of injury.”

Stretching after your warm-up is important, too, but just be careful not to overdo it. “If you stretch too aggressively, you can actually predispose yourself to muscle tendon injuries,” says Forsythe. “First warm up, and then stretch out within your range of comfort. But right before a game is not the time to all of a sudden correct tight hamstrings.”

Often, being sidelined by an injury can be more painful than the injury itself, causing guys to get back out there earlier than they probably should. “A common issue that I see is when someone sustains a minor sprain or strain, and they return to sport-specific activity too early,” says Chen, “which can result in either worsening the injury or even picking up a secondary injury.” As annoying as it might be to sit out for 2 or 3 weeks with a strained hamstring, turning that into a tear will bench you for far longer. Believe me.

Playing sports in your 30s, 40s, and beyond also means coming to grips with your body’s increasing need for routine recovery between training sessions and games. "You have to recognize that your body needs more time to recover,” says Forsythe. You may have great cardiovascular fitness and feel ready to play on consecutive days, but your muscles and connective tissues need time to bounce back. “It’s important to respect fatigue, and ensure proper recovery after games or training,” says McDonald.

To be fair, this is universally sound guidance regardless of age. But it's advice that tends to take decades to sink in. “I think that one of the key advantages of playing as you get older is that you know your body better in your 30s and 40s,” Brian’s response concluded. “You understand what it's saying to you now. You might not have even listened when you were 21!”

A version of this story appeared in British GQ.

#6642. All About Anthony De La Torre, Lana Condor’s Actor/Musician Husband

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In the To All the Boys films, Lana Condor’s character is often consumed by relationship drama. In any given movie, Lara Jean may be torn between her current boyfriend Peter Kavinsky (Noah Centineo) and childhood crush John Ambrose McClaren (Jordan Fisher), or struggling with whether to follow Peter to college. But in real life, Condor faces no such dilemma. She’s been in a relationship with actor/musician Anthony De La Torre since 2015. In January 2022, the two got engaged, and in October 2024, they got married. Below, all you need to know about De La Torre and his romance with Condor.

Like Condor, De La Torre is an actor who most famously played a young Jack Sparrow in 2017’s Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales. He’s also appeared in episodes of the Nickelodeon series 100 Things to Do Before High School and the Starz show Vida.

The couple actually met at an entertainment industry function. During her February 2019 cover story with Cosmopolitan, Condor spoke about meeting De La Torre at an Emmy nominees reception in 2015. His pickup line? “Hi, I’m Anthony. I thought I would make a friend.” She described their initial meeting to the outlet as being “like a ­Taylor Swift song.”

Ever since their storybook meeting, De La Torre and Condor have stayed by each other’s side. The actress told Cosmopolitan UK that her beau is quite the romantic. “He writes me love letters all the time,” she told the outlet. “He’s the freaking best. He’ll leave me little messages taped to my bathroom mirror on days I have to wake up early for work. He once picked up my favorite takeout food after work and served it up properly on our kitchen table, with little sticky notes attached to each plate saying how proud of me he is.”

Both Condor and De La Torre wrote romantic Instagram posts to celebrate their fifth anniversary as a couple. In August 2020, she shared a photo of the pair cuddled up on the grass with the caption, “5 years with the man of my dreams. You are still my most favorite person in the world. You are my best friend. You have taught me how to love and to be loved, to forgive and to grow, to never give up, to be each others teammate and cheerleader. You make me laugh like no other and it doesn’t matter where we are in the world, as long as I’m with you, I’m home. I love you @anthonydltorre happy anniversary. Let’s cuddle. 🐶”

De La Torre’s post, also shared on August 31, includes a sunset picture. He wrote, “5 years ago we went on our first date and saw a movie called The Gift. While the plot of the film in no way represents our life, the name of the movie couldn’t be more fitting to what you are. The greatest gift I've ever been blessed and entrusted with. From our tiny ass apartment with a blow up twin mattress to riding horses in Kenya, it has always been an adventure 🤪 Thank you for changing my life, inspiring me to grow, and making everything worth it. I love you, my tiny burrito 🌯♥️”

Condor shared the news that De La Torre popped the question on Jan. 28, 2022. She explained the details behind the ring and shared engagement photos, which you can view here on her Instagram.

She wrote, of the proposal, “Saying YES was the easiest decision I’ve ever made. I consider myself the absolute luckiest woman alive to live in your sphere. Aside from my father, without a doubt, you are the greatest man in the world. Emmy & Timmy said it’s about time mommy & daddy got engaged!!!”

Condor added of the ring, “💍: Anthony worked with the INCREDIBLE Vietnamese female owned @parisjewellerscanada to design the most stunning piece I’ve ever seen! The fact he knew how important it was to me that he’d collaborate w/ a Vietnamese company to help design my ring is a testament to just how truly thoughtful he always is. I cannot wait to be your wife, baby. I love you a million times over.”

The couple got married in Malibu at the Serra Franciscan Retreat Center, according to Vogue. Condor told the publication that she and her late mother Mary went to a spiritual retreat there when she was in high school.

“My mother Mary recently passed away, leaving my entire family devastated,” the actress shared. “But she would not have wanted us to not celebrate our love. We really wanted to get married at the Serra Retreat because being there was such a core memory that I had with my mom, and I felt like we would be able to feel her presence on our wedding night.”

The bride wore a strapless Vera Wang dress she picked out with her mother as well.

“My mom and I absolutely fell in love with my wedding gown the moment I tried it on, and I am so grateful I got to share that experience with her,” she said. “That was the only time she was able to see me in my dress, and I will hold that memory in my heart forever.”

She added, “The entire weekend could not have gone better. We are so filled with love and gratitude for each other and also for all of our incredible guests who came from far and wide to join us in the celebrations. This weekend will forever go down as the happiest weekend of our lives.”

The couple kicked off the year at Vanity Fair and Amazon MGM Studios’ awards season celebration in Los Angeles on January 10.

Condor wore a black Sebastian Gunawan Signature off-the-shoulder gown, while De La Torre opted for a copper-colored suit.

On March 15, they attended the Elton John AIDS Foundation’s annual Academy Awards viewing party in West Hollywood. Condor chose an ivory Alberta Ferretti halter-neck gown, while De La Torre wore a light blue suit.

They stepped out again on July 28 for a Los Angeles screening of The Devil’s Mouth, with Condor wearing a red gown featuring a plunging, draped neckline and De La Torre dressed in a black suit.

The pair also attended the US Open in New York City on September 8. Condor wore a navy top layered over a plaid collared shirt, accessorized with pink-tinted sunglasses, while De La Torre wore a blue blazer over a checked shirt.

In a Nov. 10, 2026 interview with People, Condor and De La Torre revealed that they spent their second wedding anniversary filming The Receipt, an upcoming romantic comedy that lets them share a love story on-screen, too.

“It was so cute. We got to celebrate it on set together with Fetch,” Condor said. “I don’t think we really told anyone. I think they just kind of knew and they were so, so sweet and everyone on set was just the most adorable. It was the cutest love-filled day. It was delightful.”

While they’ve worked together on music before, playing a couple on-screen was a new experience for Condor.

“I’ve fallen in love on camera quite a few times, but I think it’s a lot different when you can actually do it with someone that you share your life with and that you’ve loved for a very long time,” she said.

In addition to being an up-and-coming actor, De La Torre is also a musician. He’s previously been in bands including DE LA TORRE and The Fell. In October 2019, he released a new song titled “Know Me.” According to Seventeen, the track was written about Condor.

De La Torre and Condor teased the release of a joint musical project on Jan. 7, 2020. She shared a photo of the couple snuggled near a laptop on Instagram and captioned it, “We’ve been working on a very special project for months now for you guys. It’s been blood, sweat, and tears. It’s been highs & lows & sobs & laughs but we’ve done it together, and that’s what counts 💪🏽. Building dreams together. Love your loved ones, love your strangers. We can’t wait to share with you so soon x.”

Speculation that the couple was working on music together grew after De La Torre’s cryptic Instagram post. “Feb 19,” he captioned a shot of the pair.

The answer to questions about Condor and De La Torre’s first collaboration arrived with the dreamy duet, “Raining in London.” Condor announced the release of their song (and De La Torre’s EP) on Instagram. “This is our heart,” she wrote. “Our song 'Raining In London' (ft. me) is FINALLY OUT, and so is my dear @anthonydltorre whole EP FIND ME. I couldn’t be more proud of him. Against so many odds, he’s made this EP come to life for you all to hear. It’s definitely playing on repeat all day for me 💕! I love you golden boy, thru and thru.”

De La Torre also has his own channel, which includes a video of fun facts about the actor. In it, he opens up about learning to speak Spanish, his close bond with his siblings, and why he once dyed his hair black.

In the months since their first duet, the couple recorded a cover of Lauv’s “I Like Me Better” and released another original song, “No Way.” They even choreographed a TikTok dance for the latter song.

As for Condor’s musical catalog, she has also drawn inspiration from De La Torre. Last August, she released the song “For Real,” a track about how much she misses her longtime boyfriend while traveling for work.

“I’ve been in a pretty serious relationship for five years now, and whenever I travel I have to leave him,” she explained to People. “I always have a lot of anxiety about going off and leaving my home. I had just written down this journal entry about my feelings of going back to work as things start to shoot again, and my anxieties about leaving my boyfriend and about starting life up again, especially in this insane year that we've been having.”

Condor went on to address her new musical collaborations with De La Torre: “I mean, it seems so random, but I’ve always loved music. My boyfriend is a musician, and I’ve watched him navigate the music industry for years now, and I have always been very fascinated with it. I just felt like during quarantine, why not try something new if you love it?”

Condor told Cosmopolitan that when To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before was released in 2018, rumors about her and Centineo’s offscreen relationship persisted. “Noah and I definitely encouraged the speculation,” she admitted. “But it’s because we believe in the story and the characters, and we genuinely love each other. You can truly love someone in a very platonic way.”

But Condor said Instagram trolls would say “horrible things” about her real-life romance with De La Torre. “It was so hurtful for both of us,” she explained. “This is supposed to be a good thing. Why are you ­coming for someone who has no part of this story? If you say you support me, why would you hurt someone I love?”

For a while, De La Torre disabled his Instagram comments. But now, the couple seems to be handling social media pressure in stride. In August 2019, De La Torre even jokingly shared a photo with himself and Centineo, followed by a pic of Condor and co-star Madelaine Arthur. He captioned the post, “PK and LJ are even cuter in person.”

When De La Torre isn’t writing Condor love letters or sonnets, he’s providing another public service. Namely, he’s sharing photos with his and Condor’s dog Emmy. Yes, she has an Instagram:

Each couple experienced isolation a little differently during the COVID-19 pandemic. For Condor and De La Torre, they tried out TikTok trends and wore matching tie-dye outfits. Last March, both of the performers shared videos of themselves experimenting on the app to Instagram.

#6641. 22 Best Airbnbs in Upstate New York for a Weekend Away from the City 2026

If you live in New York, pretty much anything qualifies as an excuse for a weekend Upstate. A clanging radiator blasting dry heat into your apartment when it’s still warm outside? Time to flee to greener pastures. An overwhelming work week spent mostly in the company of your inbox? You deserve to unplug. The very first hint of a reddening leaf in the park? A seasonal sign from above—get yourself to an apple orchard.

With most small towns within a few hours’ drive of the city (and several available on a train line, for those without a car), you don’t really need a reason to spend a few days in Upstate New York. And while there are plenty of boutique hotels dotting the Hudson Valley and the Catskills, for true relaxation, why not book an Airbnb?

This time of year is all about the outdoors. Spend your days hiking along mountain trails and creeks, exploring local markets to sample all the fresh produce (and the baked goods they inspire), or hitting a brewery in the evening for a glass of cider under twinkling lights. As the weather cools, the charm offensive continues: fire pits come out, farms open for pumpkin and apple harvesting, and following the foliage becomes a perfectly acceptable way to spend a lazy fall day. Some of our favorite Upstate New York Airbnbs are located in or within walking distance of quaint towns like Hudson and Woodstock; though if you prefer a truly off-the-grid experience, we found plenty of cabins and cottages surrounded only by meadows.

Ahead, the 22 best Airbnbs in Upstate New York.

Enjoy a slower pace at this newly renovated 1890s-era farmhouse in the Western Catskills. The home is set on 25 acres of rolling meadows and forest, which lead to two streams and a waterfall. While the home has been updated to feature all new appliances (including a Vitamix), details like reclaimed wood and a bread-baking wood-stove cement the snug vibes. The main area is one big room: an eight-person dining room table connects to the kitchen, where you can spend afternoons making the most of local ingredients you picked up from a nearby farmstand. And when you head upstairs, don’t miss the claw-foot tub—it’s reason enough to book this gorgeous stay.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 5

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, window AC unit, heating, indoor fireplace, backyard, outdoor dining area.

This spot is billed as a “boutique nature retreat”—but let’s call it what it really is: an adult treehouse. It sleeps two, with a king-sized bed and hot outdoor showers. With no cell service or electricity, this is your chance to go fully off the grid; since the whole house is surrounded by forest, you’ll feel completely cozy and secluded. When you want to re-join society, the town of Phoenicia (and, more importantly, the local favorite Phoenicia Diner) is just a 10-minute drive away.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, fire pit, free parking

Best For: Fulfilling childhood treehouse dreams.

“Upstate” in perhaps only the most abstract sense of the word (it borders New Jersey, just about one hour out of the city), this lakeside spot is filled with sunlight, a far cry from the heavy wooden cabins that permeate the area. Outside, there’s a private garden with a waterfall and lily pond—and, of course, those unbeatable views of Greenwood Lake. There are plenty of wineries and antique stores nearby, as well as hikes for the adventurous weekender (the home is a five-minute walk from a path that connects to the Appalachian Trail) and a massive claw-foot tub to soak in when it’s time to unwind.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: HDTV, bathtub, record player, crib, board games, wood-burning fireplace, patio, outdoor furniture

Best For: Those who crave nature, but are afraid of the whole cabin-in-the-woods idea.

Renovated for modernity but restored with heaps of vintage touches befitting the older home’s roots, this light-filled apartment right in the heart of Hudson is great if you prefer to stay in a town rather than remote wilderness. From the zellige tiles to the antique stove, the kitchen is a particular star—anyone looking for style inspiration for an upcoming remodel will find several nooks to bookmark here. The Nespresso and tea station helps you start each morning off on a caffeinated foot, while in the afternoons, you’ll want to hang out on the porch or in the bubblegum pink claw-foot tub with a book.

Amenities: TV, sound system, crib, patio.

This new listing is the epitome of stripped-back country living: There’s no television and few amenities, so if you’re looking for a spot to indulge your off-the-grid dreams, this is it. (Though, lest you change your mind, the hamlet of Livingston Manor, with its concept stores and coffee shops, is walking distance away.) The house is a freshly renovated farmhouse, done in the Scandinavian style—from the antique furnishings to the original wood floors, every corner is steeped in character. There’s a bunk room for the youngest members of your travel party, plus a spacious kitchen for whipping up hearty breakfasts at home before heading out for the day.

Amenities: Air conditioning, pet-friendly.

Best For: Anyone looking to truly disconnect for a weekend.

Picture the prototypical lake cottage. Wood, everywhere, is a given; as is an A-frame silhouette, a fire pit and deck for grilling, and perhaps a wood-burning fireplace or two. Welcome to the Airbnb embodiment of that vision, complete with all of the above plus a few modern amenities (the Nespresso machine is a welcome addition). Sleepy Hollow Lake is a quick 10-minute walk down a trail away, for summertime guests. In the colder months, Hunter mountain and its ski slopes are a 45-minute drive away; and in between, you’ll have a third of an acre worth of land to explore on the property itself.

Amenities: Bathtub, record player, high chair, travel crib, board games, fireplace, beach/lake access, fire pit, pet friendly.

Distance from NYC: 2 hours by train, 2.5 hours by car.

No car, no problem: This charming one-bedroom is right in the town of Cold Spring, easily reachable from the city via the Metro North. You’ll be able to walk everywhere (Cold Spring Coffeehouse, a must-visit for your morning cappuccino and cardamom bun, is just 15 minutes on foot) and spend your weekend like a local. The home itself is clean and minimally decorated, with just enough original touches—including a gorgeous fireplace—to keep it from feeling too sparse. Remote workers will appreciate the spacious dining table, too, which doubles as a workspace you can spread out in in a picturesque alcove.

Distance from NYC: 1.5 hours by car, 1.5 hours by train.

Inspired by a Swiss Alpine home, this modern space is compact and minimalist, with oversized windows that really let the mountainside views seep in. Take it in up close and personal on the (covered) patio, which, in warmer months, is a great spot for a breakfast or dinner. Indoors, a colorful kitchen, shower skylight, and pellet stove all make for memorable decorative touches. It’s the right size for a solo traveler or a couple looking for a short-term stay; you’ll have all the necessities you need, but you’re encouraged to make the most of your surroundings.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, pellet stove, patio, fire pit, EV charger, pet-friendly.

Distance from NYC: Around 3 hours by train.

Best For: The no-frills traveler who still appreciates a little aesthetic effort.

Built in the ’80s by a master stonemason, this is one of the more unique options available to Catskills travelers. The home is actually a tower, with vaulted ceilings and wraparound windows offering sweeping views of the valley below. (The bathtub on the second floor is an especially great spot to take them in.) Just a quick seven-minute drive to the town of Woodstock, you’ll be left alone but not fully remote. And if it’s still warm enough, be sure to factor in enough free time for some evenings spent outdoors—the views are incredible, and between the hot tub and the deck, there are plenty of spots to take them in.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Washer/dryer, bathtub, piano, record player, board games, air conditioning, fireplace, fire pit, hot tub.

Best For: Someone who read one too many fairytale books growing up.

This charming A-frame in Tannersville is full of lush plants, good energy, and nostalgic charm. The home dates back to 1971 and is right in the heart of the Catskills, just two hours north of New York City. While the interiors are supremely serene, the outdoor deck with its BBQ and twinkly lights is where you’ll probably spend most of your time—especially if you’re visiting in fall or spring, when the weather is its mildest. Prefer to stay in? The home comes stocked with a record player and board games, for cozy nights with the whole group that are probably why you booked an Airbnb Upstate in the first place.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating, backyard, BBQ.

Best For: Plant parents who need a getaway.

If the idea of staying in a cabin in the woods with a cedar wood-fired hot tub sounds up your alley, book a stay at this bright home just 10 minutes from Woodstock. It’s not quite your old-school cottage: Aside from the light palette and modern decor, the bedrooms feature Casper mattresses, and the Breville espresso machine will make morning coffees on the deck all the more enjoyable. Outside, a fire pit and cedar wood hot tub and sauna make the case for ditching the dinner reservation in favor of staying in; plus, the house comes with a movie projector, for DIY movie nights.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, AC, central heating, backyard, fire pit, hammock, BBQ, hot tub.

Best For: A soak in the hot tub, beneath the trees.

From the wood-paneled A-frame ceilings to the forest green paint theme to the coffee-colored zellige tiling in the bathroom, there are plenty of decor ideas to steal from this Airbnb. Design aside, it’s well-located (hop in the car for a quick drive to the Ashokan Reservoir and little towns like Kingston and Woodstock) and surprisingly spacious. Come summer, we predict you’ll want to spend all your time on the sprawling front deck overlooking the trees—ditto the fall, as long as you pack the appropriate amount of wool sweaters to stay warm.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit, outdoor furniture, patio, pet-friendly.

We can already feel our blood pressure lowering simply admiring this tranquil Airbnb located on the outskirts of Kingston. The property offers numerous nooks for experiencing the natural surroundings—a fire pit encircled by Adirondack chairs, a tranquil pond best savored from the home’s swinging hammock, and even a screened porch just off the kitchen for early morning coffee. Inside is equally as dreamy, with plenty of natural light and cozy touches like exposed brick and a small fireplace. One perk: You can bring your pups for a small fee, so no member of the family is left behind for the next weekend Upstate.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard, fire pit, hammock, BBQ.

Hide yourself away in this atmospheric cabin perched atop Bramley Mountain near Bovina Center, a great spot for cozy restaurants and country stores. The home has a spacious atmosphere thanks to the cathedral ceilings and open floor plan, but you never lose that innately cozy feel: a wood-burning stove, wood paneling, and an atmospheric porch are all there to remind you that you’re very much in the woods. Not that there’s a bad time to book a stay here, but if you have your pick, aim for the fall. The house is surrounded by trees that turn surreal shades of scarlet and persimmon come October.

Amenities: Bathtub, outdoor shower, washer/dryer, indoor fireplace, backyard.

Best For: Turning your phone on airplane mode.

There are two types of upstate getaways: the first, characterized by spending the entire weekend in one place, relaxing and recharging. The second is spent diving headfirst into the region’s many charms, exploring shops, restaurants, and markets in several small towns. This Airbnb is ideal for the latter sort of traveler, who wants friction-less access to destinations such as Woodstock, Saugerties, and Kingston.

It also happens to be impeccably designed, with highlights like an indoor fireplace, mid-century modern decor, and a backyard BBQ and fire pit you’ll have a hard time parting ways with—it even comes stocked with firewood.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, indoor fireplace, fire pit, hammock, BBQ.

Best For: Exploring several nearby towns (and an impromptu game of chess to end the night).

Leaning into Wabi-Sabi design, this ranch-style home in the Warwick Valley is close to several lakes and hiking trails (as well as trendy breweries and restaurants). Natural materials and soft lighting set a relaxed tone for the space, and a trip to The Shed (the home’s meditation room) for a yoga session will begin each day on the right foot, as will the complimentary freshly-roasted bag of ground coffee from the owner’s favorite purveyor, Voyager Espresso. When you’re living in the foreground of the dense green forest, visible from most windows in the home, it’s impossible to not feel zen.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, yoga studio, central AC and heating, lake access, fire pit, backyard, BBQ, EV charger.

Best For: Coming back from your vacation actually recharged.

This secluded sanctuary in the Catskills forest sits on a hill overlooking an abundance of beauty, from woodlands and stream-fed ponds to a sprawling wildflower meadow. The cabin is petite (just 400 square feet) but a Wabi Sabi-inspired design lends a calming effect. A few standout details—and there are several—include the open floor plan with a winding spiral staircase in the center, natural earthy textures throughout, and a peaceful outdoor area complete with a fire pit, picnic tables, and twinkly lights. Even the bedroom is impeccably designed, with its antique chair nightstand and matching bedding; twin beds have never looked chicer.

Amenities: Toiletries, washer/dryer, record player, books and board games, window AC unit, indoor pellet stove, kitchen, fire pit, charcoal BBQ.

Best For: Reading your book beneath a canopy of trees.

Think of the typical log house, then flip that idea on its head. That’s what you get with Fox Ridge Chalet, which is anything but ordinary: A lot of it is white-washed, making it feel even bigger and brighter than it is, and the assortment of furniture is so eclectic, it has the air of a cool vintage shop. Situated on seven private acres of land, the picturesque property beckons to be explored. For the days when you decide you want to stay in, the movie screening projector, pool table, hot tub, exercise bike, and game collection should more than suffice.

Amenities: Hot tub, pool table, exercise equipment, fire pit, outdoor furniture, grill

Best For: Multigenerational summer getaways with the family.

Part of the National Register of Historic Places, this residence dubbed “The Gatehouse” was last restored in 2016—updated with more modern decor and comfy furnishings. Immerse yourself in scenic views of the Catskills Mountains and Hudson River from this historic French home while relaxing in the backyard, where a separate carriage house offers covered outdoor dining for the colder months. (Or the front yard—that storybook-perfect porch demands a few mornings or afternoons spend lounging on it.) Stay occupied with limitless activities such as hiking, biking, boating, and antique shopping, all of which can be found in the historic town of Hyde Park.

Amenities: Private balcony/patio, indoor fireplace, outdoor dining area, fire pit, BBQ grill

Best For: Staying in a home on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Pond House is a property with some serious art history cachet: It’s the former studio of social realist painter Reginald Marsh. An architect lovingly restored it into a single-family home that exudes country elegance: there are exposed beam ceilings, chandeliers, and floor-to-ceiling windows that look out onto the estate’s pond. Its most unique selling point is the main bedroom: With floor-to-ceiling glass windows slotted into wood paneling, you get a front row seat to the great outdoors from the comfort of your bed. It’ll be like sleeping in the world’s most relaxing fishbowl. (The adjacent bathroom, with its spa-like tub and equally oversized windows, is a nice companion.)

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 5

Amenities: private balcony, bathtub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

If you’re traveling with a large group (or looking for a spot to stay around a wedding), this home can fit over 16 guests. It’s the perfect luxurious weekend getaway—perched upon a sprawling 16 acres, this converted-barn home has a design-forward interior complete with 30-foot ceilings as well as five-and-a-half bedrooms. The service is also top-notch, as the property comes with a 24-hour digital concierge as well as a private chef upon request. You’ll only be a few minutes from Woodstock village, if you want to venture out for breakfast before heading out to traverse the area’s many hiking trails.

Rooms: 5 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms; sleeps 16+

Amenities: private hot tub, indoor fireplace, hammock, private balcony, patio and backyard

Best For: A grand fireplace that will take your breath away.

The sister property to the earlier Hudson home in our edit (all designed by New York design firm Zio & Sons), this three-bedroom offers a little more space. It’s a charming townhouse in the Hudson Valley right by the main stretch of shops and restaurants, chock full of antiques and old-world details like salvaged library doors in the bedroom and an 1840s-era mantel. This is a spot to save if you love design—from the cast iron tub to the copper pan-lined tile kitchen to the original wallpaper in the living room, the home is brimming with inspiration at every turn.

Amenities: private balcony/patio, bathtub, outdoor dining area,

Distance From NYC: 2 hours by car and train.

Best For: A design-driven stay in Hudson.

#6640. 31 Thanksgiving Desserts to Cap Your Holiday Feast

There’s Thanksgiving dinner, and then there are Thanksgiving desserts. These are two separate events, and in between, it’s perfectly fine to take a disco nap. (In fact, we recommend it.)

“This is the magnum opus of Thanksgiving dessert recipes,” writes one reader whose 90-year-old grandfather asked for a repeat performance. “You bet your boots I will—it’s the best apple pie, ever.”

A colossal, self-serve mousse is a baller host move—no tidy slicing, no fussy garnishing, no jockeying for oven space. Set out bowls and spoons and let guests help themselves. Vanilla lovers, try our Colossal Crème Brûlée.

Butter-toasted pecans get the glory, but sour cream does the work, balancing both the gooey pecan layer and the pile of whipped cream. Between them? A thick layer of silky brown sugar custard.

A slice of Thanksgiving pie is nice, but how about a slice of pumpkin flan under a veneer of caramel? This one takes a page from Puerto Rican flan de queso, with cream cheese lending richness, tang, and luxurious texture.

Consider this pie a tangy exclamation point to the holiday meal: cranberry-lime curd in a flaky cream cheese crust, crowned with billows of meringue.

Brown sugar takes some of the fuss out of caramel cake’s famously finicky frosting while browned butter adds toasty depth. Spread it over tender yellow cake layers and finish with flaky salt.

Silky filling, flaky crust, a whisper of spice: This is pumpkin pie done right. Sweetened condensed milk gives the custard its richness; maple syrup and vanilla round out the flavor.

Skip the rolling pin: Buttered phyllo encloses an orange-scented custard, with crumpled sheets forming a dramatically ruffled top. Cinnamon sugar adds crunch to this no-roll pie.

This plush pumpkin spice cake wears a thick swoop of tangy cream cheese frosting. Bake the cake a day ahead, then add the frosting in the lull between dinner and dessert.

If most holiday desserts feel a tad too sweet for you, herbal rosemary and fruity olive oil give this cake just enough savory elements to justify a second helping.

Blanketing quartered apples with rough-puff pastry feels rustic enough, but once baked and inverted, this shimmering, blushing tart dominates the holiday table.

Sweet potato, warming spices, and orange zest get a gloss of dark chocolate in this autumnal loaf cake. Bake it up to three days ahead, leaving the ganache for later.

A deeply browned top and cracked sides are the goal here, not a baking mishap. Underneath: a custardy, pumpkin-spiced cheesecake that needs neither a crust nor a water bath.

Pecan pie meets Hawaiian-style butter mochi in this chewy, coconut-milk-rich cake. Miso-and-maple-coated pecans bring salty-sweet crunch, with some sinking into the batter as the cake bakes.

This date cake blanketed in toffee sauce tastes like cozying up by the fireside after a game of football on the lawn. Bake the unsauced cake a day ahead, then rewarm before finishing.

Cinnamon-spiced pumpkin cake rolled around walnut-studded cream cheese filling needs little embellishment. A dusting of powdered sugar is plenty—each slice supplies its own dramatic swirl.

This glamorous layer cake, with jewel-toned swipes of cranberry jam, white chocolate–cream cheese frosting, and sugared cranberries, looks and tastes like winter is coming (in the best possible way).

A no-bake Oreo crust, a rich chocolate filling, and a tower of whipped cream come together in this shut-the-room-up dessert.

Caramel-glazed apple halves crown this nutty upside-down cake, all baked in the same skillet used to brown the fruit. A scoop of vanilla ice cream on top? We wouldn’t say no.

A floral, earthy saffron soak gives this sponge cake a pudding-like texture and its vibrant yellow color, while pistachios add nutty crunch.

Inspired by the flavors of a pumpkin spice latte, this rendition of old-school tiramisu calls for soaking ladyfingers in bourbon-spiked espresso, then enveloping them in plumes of pumpkin-mascarpone cream.

Cranberries with dinner and again for dessert? Absolutely. Tart filling hides between layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust in this Linzer tart. Prefer individual portions? Try these cranberry hand pies.

Pumpkin crumb cake is like the brownie of Thanksgiving desserts: easy to tote and slice for sharing. Here, sweet rice flour gives the cake a chewy bounce beneath a buttery, crispy-crumbly pecan streusel.

The ultraflaky crust barely contains the lofty, fudgy almond filling, but have faith: It will puff and dome as it bakes, then settle back into sliceable form once cool.

Alternate layers of pumpkin and chocolate batter create this Bundt cake’s mesmerizing marbling—no knife-swirling necessary. A blanket of chocolate ganache makes it equally appealing to the pumpkin crowd and the chocolate diehards.

Whole roasted birds, spatchcocked showstoppers, braised legs, breasts for smaller gatherings, and more ways to put turkey at the center of the table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

Squishy rolls for mopping up gravy, flaky biscuits for piling on leftover turkey, and a seedy pumpkin loaf to start the day.

From hot toddies to big-batch punch, these festive drinks will get you in the holiday spirit.

#6637. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6636. Lara Saget’s Sculptures Mine the Ancient, Alchemical, and Divine

On the way to Lara Saget’s Brooklyn studio, I see a headstone shop, where grave markers are displayed in the window. On the next block, there’s a warehouse, its open garage doors revealing floor-to-ceiling stacks of granite and marble slabs. And inside, her studio is a bit of a quarry itself.

“This is my rock room,” the 37-year-old sculptor says, gesturing to a corner of her studio that looks like a construction site. “This is where I collect all my different little things.” She points to a pile of gray stone, explaining that it is rare Tuckahoe marble, which was used to build the Washington Square arch. When Saget saw that a hotel was set to be built on a former Tuckahoe marble quarry in Westchester County, she called the owner and asked if she could come collect some.

This practice of seeing the sublime in nature is at the heart of Saget’s practice: She sees the divine in granite, the sacred in destruction that makes way for creation. These are themes she mines in her first New York City solo exhibition, “and the world came apart,” curated by Sarah Darro, which opened at Trotter&Sholer on November 7. Saget is exhibiting the work after recently receiving her master’s in divinity from the Center for Religion and Advanced Spiritual Studies and becoming an ordained minister. This spirituality deeply informs the work, which is about regeneration, the ancient, and the alchemical.

Lara Saget, The Children and the Tree That Turned to Metal, 2026. Copper alloy and petrified wood. 11 x 6 x 3 in.

The show, which variously brings to mind the celestial sculptures of Lee Bontecou and the arresting imagery of Louise Bourgeois, has two components: wall works made from copper alloy, granite, and black marble that borrow the aesthetics of early cave drawings to depict volcanic maps and tectonic plates; and glass sculptures centered on the ancient Judean date palm, a once-extinct tree scientists were able to regenerate from nearly 2,000-year-old seeds, and the Joshua Tree, which is threatened by climate change.

Saget has a broader interest in legacy and inheritance. As the daughter of the late actor Bob Saget, she inherited not just a famous last name, but also the example from an early age of what it looks like to be an artist. Now, almost five years after his death, a documentary about him is in the works. “He was a true artist,” she says. “He was like jazz, just like this constant creation. Being surrounded by that has made it seem very normal to be constantly creating.”

In 2019, she traveled to India for the first time, spending a month in a small village at Art Ichol, a residency for artists working in bronze and stone. Saget has gone back almost every year since to make her work, which involves a 6,000-year-old process called “lost-wax casting.” She works with a team to carve into stone and use wax to make a print of its surface. She then builds a mold around the wax and stone, and constructs a kind of sweat lodge out of bricks and mud to steam out the wax, leaving a cavity for molten metal to be poured in. Every step of the process is manual.

Saget has had a lifelong interest in spirituality, but it wasn’t until the last decade, when she found the Path of Soul Transcendence, that she began to pursue it more seriously. “Honestly, my whole life, I was looking for something,” she says. “The experience of the path is really surrendering to the spirit that I am, that everybody is, and the reality that everything is one.”

It’s an idea essential to her practice, which is rooted in how materials interact with each other. “I just had the sense that when heat breaks everything down, it's all ultimately one,” Saget says. “The center of the earth, or how volcanoes are also obsidian rock, and how all these materials are basically everything. It seems like it’s totally separate, but when it's heated, it reveals it's not.”

Saget’s wall works take a bird’s-eye view, using a tiled-grid modularity that evokes sites of excavation and discovery. The Last One Million Years (2026), for example, is a map of volcanoes and tectonic plates she charted using a celestial map from NASA. The raised rock parts of the maps are from heat-trapping granite in the metal, a spontaneous interaction. The effect is a kind of spiritual archaeology, wherein Saget uses the earth’s most ancient, essential materials to tap into its profundities.

Lara Saget, Joshua, 2026. Kiln-cast glass and phosphorescent powder, 15.5 × 6 × 6 in.

If the wall works are the story of the last million years, Saget’s tree sculptures are the story of the present and future. She started making glass tree sculptures in 2016, focusing on trees that have survived against all odds. She began sculpting Joshua trees during the pandemic, when she drove across the country to Yucca Valley Material Lab in Joshua Tree for a residency. While she was there, it snowed—a rare occurrence—which made her think about how the Joshua tree survived the Ice Age. Similarly, the sculpture Rebirth of an Ancient Palm is a recreation of the ancient Judean date palm, which was brought back to life from extinction. Both sculptures feature textural, kiln-cast glass using the lost-wax process. For the exhibition, she had two children narrate an audio piece, each acting as one of the trees and encouraging people to take care of them. “Nobody could imagine that these trees could survive all of this,” she says. “It’s really about the underlying life force that continues against all cognitive understanding.”

Indeed, she’s begun to think about grief in similar terms. “Working through what seemed to be finite, and allowing what seemed finite to almost reveal itself as infinite has helped a lot,” Saget says. “Because I realized that nothing is the end of anything. It’s always in the process of becoming.”

“and the world came apart,” runs through December 19 at Trotter&Sholer at 90 Elizabeth Street in New York City.

#6634. Denis Villeneuve Is GQ’s Director of the Year

Where some other awards-bestowing committees have been notoriously late in giving great directors their flowers, GQ refuses to waste time. Which is why we’ve honored Denis Villeneuve as our Director of the Year for 2026—yes, for Dune: Part Three, due out December 18th, but also for turning a Hollywood-stymying sci-fi classic into a three-part visual feast that we wish didn’t have to end. So before it does, GQ will be celebrating Villeneuve tonight, in Los Angeles.

The French-Canadian is, of course, more than just the director of Dune. He’s an Academy Award winner who can turn tentpole spectacles into critical darlings. As GQ’s Zach Baron writes in his profile of Villeneuve, out next week, “His signature films—2015’s cartel thriller Sicario, or 2016’s science fiction film Arrival, which was nominated for eight Academy Awards—are knotty and severe and not always easy to follow; they are also beautiful and seem to play well anywhere, whether on an airplane, in an HBO rerun, or at an IMAX theater.”

He is also, now, about to embark on another massive adventure, though this time in our solar system: Villeneuve will be directing the next James Bond film.

To celebrate the man behind the camera, GQ will host a conversation between Villeneuve and Zach Baron, host of One More Question, followed by a special screening of Dune: Part Two to get everyone ready for the third-and-final installment. This all happens tonight at the newly opened, architecturally stunning Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles.

Come back next Tuesday to read Baron’s profile of Denis Villeneuve, part of GQ’s Men of the Year issue.

#6633. The World's 50 Best Restaurants, According to ‘The 50’ Best List

Asador Etxebarri from the Spanish Basque Country won the title of world's best restaurant Wednesday night when The 50, the organization formerly known as 50 Best, announced its annual ranking during a ceremony in Lima, Peru. It was the first such event for The 50 in South America.

Situated between Bilbao and San Sebastián, Etxebarri claims some of the world's most famous chefs as major fans of Bittor Arginzoniz, who matches the characteristics of the wood in the grill with the plants and proteins sizzling over the flames. It was No. 2 on The 50 in 2025 and maintains one Michelin star. Tasting menus are around $337.

Wednesday was also a big night for Atomix in New York, which came in at No. 11 and was named Best Restaurant in North America. Junghyun Park took home the Chef's Choice Award.

A spot on The 50 is among the highest honors a restaurant can receive. (Disclosure: Bon Appétit editor in chief Jamila Robinson is a 50 Best Academy Chair.) The list favors some of the most expensive, elaborate cooking in the fine-dining world. It often rewards tasting menus that employ molecular gastronomy, but also celebrates the simple elegance of a Spanish grill, the sourcing mission of an Argentine steakhouse, or the laidback cool of Parisian neo-bistro.

This year’s ceremony ran into controversy earlier in the year when it was announced that it would be hosted in Abu Dhabi, which has faced criticism for human rights violations. In June, it was announced that the ceremony would instead be hosted in Peru, home to Maido, the Lima restaurant that won No. 1 last year. Maido is not eligible for this year’s list. After winning the top spot, it moves to the organization’s Best of the Best list alongside other past number ones like Barcelona’s Disfrutar and New York’s Eleven Madison Park.

Quintonil landed at No. 4. The two-Michelin starred restaurant in Mexico City led by Jorge Vallejo and Alejandra Flores, serves dishes that revolve around local, pre-Hispanic ingredients, which come together in energized and unexpected ways throughout its multi-course prix-fixe menu. A November menu listed on its website was priced around $327 per person for a meal that included lobster in a pipián verde with makrut lime, and an heirloom white corn tamal made with ayocote beans and young corn cream.

At Alchemist in Copenhagen (No. 3), chef Rasmus Munk oversees a meal that skews sci-fi with dishes that mimic brains and eyeballs and a show that advertises “up to 50 impressions,” both edible and “purely experiential.” It holds two Michelin stars and was ranked fifth on The 50 last year.

Gaggan in Bangkok (No. 2) claimed the title of Asia's Best Restaurant behind the creative, genre-bending Indian cooking of Gaggan Anand.

Critics of the World’s 50 Best have raised questions around its voting practices, which do not demand that voters pay for their own meals. The organization, for its part, explains that the list is voted on by more than 1,100 voters across 28 regions, a quarter of whom are new each year. The voting body is made up of equal parts chefs and restaurateurs, food writers, and “well-travelled gourmets,” as the The 50 website puts it. Aside from the Academy Chairs, voters must remain anonymous.

There is no set criteria for what makes a restaurant the best, and “every style of restaurant in the world is eligible,” though the list skews completely towards high-end dining even as other best-of links have begun to include street food venues, for instance.

Ana Ros, the chef at three Michelin-starred Hisa Franko in Slovenia, published a statement on Instagram last month explaining why she would not attend the ceremony in Lima. “Success within the ranking has come to depend increasingly on visibility within the system,” she wrote. “…When visibility becomes the currency, the ability to promote a restaurant in this system risks becoming as important as the work happening inside it.”

Ros, who won the award for best female chef from The 50 in 2017, told Bon Appétit that restaurants and tourism boards “more or less” know who the anonymous voters are, and they often have to make decisions about whether to pay for travel, meals, and other entertainment to try and boost their standing.

“With more rules and a little bit more control, this list can really shine again,” she said in an interview.

Hisa Franko was No. 60 on the ranking of 51-100 this year. It was 69th last year and No. 48 in 2024.

Ros said seeing her restaurant at any place on the list was “a fantastic result” and she would be wishing everyone all the best at the ceremony.

In Mexico City, gorditas are a blank canvas for creative fillings such as stringy quesillo, spiced chorizo, or even a whole fried egg.

#6632. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6631. The Vogue Business AI Tracker

The Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon launches SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The new SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils plans for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Why it matters: Zalando has announced plans for a new AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique users this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings update.

The retailer’s plans follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up new routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship.
